title: Contact Between Groups
text:
In 1954 the psychologist Gordon Allport proposed what became known as the contact hypothesis: prejudice between groups can be reduced when members meet under the right conditions, such as equal status, shared goals, cooperation and support from authorities. For decades researchers tested the idea in schools, workplaces, the military and neighborhoods around the world, with mixed impressions of how well it worked.

In 2006 Thomas Pettigrew and Linda Tropp gathered all the studies they could find. Their meta-analysis combined more than 500 studies involving more than 250,000 people in dozens of countries. The groups ranged from ethnic and racial groups to gay men and lesbians, people with disabilities, the elderly and people with mental illness.

The overall conclusion was clear. Contact between groups generally reduced prejudice, and the more rigorous the study, the stronger the effect tended to be. Contact under Allport's favorable conditions worked best, but even contact without all of them still helped. The effects also tended to spread beyond the individuals met to the group as a whole, and even to other groups. Getting to know people personally, it seemed, was one of the most reliable ways to soften hostility toward their group.
lesson: Prejudice tends to fade through real acquaintance. Seek out chances to work or spend time with people from groups you know mainly by reputation.
location: Worldwide (meta-analysis of studies from many countries)
source: Pettigrew, T. F., and Tropp, L. R. (2006). A meta-analytic test of intergroup contact theory. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 90(5), 751-783.
caveat: Later reviews note that relatively few contact studies are randomized experiments with long follow-up, so the size of lasting effects is still debated.
